entry.title: PVT-Tolerant CMOS Inverter Amplifiers Using Ring-Oscillator-Based Dynamic Voltage Scaling

link.title: PVT-Tolerant CMOS Inverter Amplifiers Using Ring-Oscillator-Based Dynamic Voltage Scaling

entry.content:
The CMOS inverter as an amplifier

The CMOS inverter, biased at mid-supply (\(V_{DD}/2\)) for maximum gain linearity, offers several benefits as an amplifier building block [1]:

  1. The input drives both devices, so the transconductances add: \(g_m = g_{mn} + g_{mp}\).
  2. It operates in class AB, which is more power efficient than a class-A stage.
  3. It has only one input node and one output node, so there are fewer parasitic poles to deal with than in, say, a folded-cascode stage.
  4. It offers the highest output swing for a given supply.

The push-pull action is also what makes the stage linear. Writing the large-signal output current as the difference of the NMOS and PMOS currents,

\[i_o = i_n - i_p = \left[k_n V_{OV,n} + k_p V_{OV,p}\right] v_i + \frac{1}{2}\left(k_n - k_p\right) v_i^2\]

where \(k = \mu C_{ox} W/L\) is the conductance constant of each device and \(V_{OV}\) its overdrive. Notice that the square term is proportional to \(k_n - k_p\). If we size \(W_n\) and \(W_p\) such that \(k_n = k_p\), the square term cancels and the output current becomes a linear function of \(v_i\), which is a rather nice result for a two-transistor circuit. Even with some mismatch, the second-order term is only proportional to the difference in the \(k\) values [1].

Noise first, linearity last

In practice, the amplifier is implemented as a cascade of gain stages. The noise requirement of the first stage matters the most. For \(n\) cascaded stages, the Friis equation gives the total noise factor as [4]

\[F_{total} = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3 - 1}{G_1 G_2} + \cdots + \frac{F_n - 1}{G_1 G_2 \cdots G_{n-1}}\]

where \(F_i\) is the (linear) noise factor of stage \(i\), with \(NF_i = 10\log_{10} F_i\), and \(G_i\) is its available power gain. Notice that the excess noise of each stage is divided by the total gain that precedes it, so after a reasonably high-gain first stage, the later stages contribute little.

Meanwhile, the signal swing grows from stage to stage, so linearity becomes more and more important further down the chain. Assuming third-order nonlinearity dominates and neglecting any phase cancellation between distortion components, the cascaded input-referred intercept is approximately [4]

\[\frac{1}{A_{IIP3,total}^2} \approx \frac{1}{A_{IIP3,1}^2} + \frac{1}{A_{v1}^2 A_{IIP3,2}^2} + \frac{1}{A_{v1}^2 A_{v2}^2 A_{IIP3,3}^2} + \cdots\]

where \(A_{IIP3,i}\) is the input intercept amplitude of stage \(i\) and \(A_{vi}\) its voltage gain. This is the mirror image of the Friis equation: each later stage’s intercept is divided by the gain before it, so its nonlinearity is effectively magnified. The largest nonlinearity contributions therefore come from the later stages.

Therefore, the first stage is optimized for noise and input matching, and the subsequent stages are optimized for linear gain and bandwidth.

The problem: an inverter has no bias current source

Skipping over the details of the amplifier implementation, we now focus on the process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) sensitivity of the inverter-based amplifier.

Traditional designs that use differential pairs have good common-mode and power-supply noise suppression. The inverter has no such immunity, and, more importantly, it is not biased by a current source; it is self-biased. Its bias current and transconductance are set entirely by the power supply and the devices themselves:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:inverter-gm} g_m \approx k V_{OV} = k\left(V_{IN} - V_T\right) = k\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{2} - V_T\right) \end{equation}

This immediately tells us where the sensitivity comes from. \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_T\) appear side by side, and the overdrive \(V_{DD}/2 - V_T\) is typically small, so a modest shift in \(V_T\) or in mobility (through \(k\)) produces a large relative change in \(g_m\). While the gain of the amplifier is somewhat stabilized by its feedback resistor, its bandwidth is primarily set by \(g_m/C\) and is therefore very sensitive to PVT. If the supply and the threshold vary, the bandwidth, and to a lesser extent the gain, of the inverter will vary significantly. Mitigating these variations is essential for a high-yield, robust design.

Why not a constant-\(g_m\) bias?

A traditional constant-\(g_m\) bias circuit consumes static current, and its devices (and therefore its power) must be scaled up to suppress random mismatch. A ring oscillator, on the other hand, consumes only dynamic power, and that power is nearly independent of the number of stages. It is therefore possible to use a large number of stages to average out random variation in the oscillation frequency [2].

Closing a loop around the supply

Since the supply sets the bias, the supply is also the natural control knob. What we want is a mechanism that detects which process corner and temperature the chip is operating at, and uses that information in a feedback loop to adjust \(V_{DD}\). For this purpose, an on-chip programmable linear regulator (LDO) is added, as shown in Figure 1 [1]. The LDO isolates the signal path from power-supply and substrate noise, and it can be calibrated so that bandwidth and gain variation across corners is minimized.

Figure 1. Schematic of the dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) scheme. The regulator output (0.75 V to 1.25 V) supplies both the 53 GBd linear TIA and the process and temperature monitor. Reproduced from Lakshmikumar et al. [1], Fig. 15. How do we detect PVT variation on the chip? Briefly put, a ring oscillator (RO) made of the same unit-sized inverter acts as a PVT sensor [1]. Its frequency depends on the same mobility and threshold voltage as the amplifier’s \(g_m\). One distinction is worth keeping in mind. The amplifier’s inverters are biased at \(V_{DD}/2\), so their overdrive is \(V_{DD}/2 - V_T\). The RO swings rail to rail, so its delay is governed by the full-supply overdrive \(V_{DD} - V_T\) (Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-delay} below). The next section shows how the two are nevertheless linked. The RO frequency is compared with an external reference clock in the frequency comparator. The digital output of the comparator then represents the process corner and temperature of the chip [1]. This digital output programs the LDO, which changes \(V_{DD}\) until the RO reaches a targeted frequency. That target represents the nominal response of the inverter (or TIA). The loop cannot change \(V_T\) or the mobility, but by adjusting the supply it compensates for their variation, so the inverter’s transconductance stays tightly controlled even as PVT varies.

The ring oscillator as a PVT sensor

When an odd number of inverters is connected in a ring, there is no stable DC operating point, and the loop satisfies the Barkhausen criterion at the frequency where the stage delays supply the remaining phase shift. The circuit therefore oscillates. Each stage’s delay is set by how long its output current takes to charge the capacitance of the next stage, roughly \(t_p \approx CV/(2I)\). The oscillation frequency is

\begin{equation} \label{eq:ro-frequency} f_{osc} = \frac{1}{2N \cdot t_p} \end{equation}

where \(N\) is the number of stages and \(t_p\) is the average inverter propagation delay [2]. The factor \(2N\) arises because one oscillation period contains \(2N\) stage transitions: each stage switches once high-to-low and once low-to-high. Similarly, the factor \(1/2\) in \(t_p \approx CV/(2I)\) reflects the fact that each output only has to swing to the next stage’s switching threshold, \(V/2\). The symmetric NMOS and PMOS drive strengths play a different role: they make the rising and falling delays nearly equal, which is why a single average \(t_p\) can be used [2].

Assuming that the gate delay is dominated by slewing and that the transistors obey the square law, the inverter delay in the RO is [2]

\begin{equation} \label{eq:ro-delay} t_p = \frac{V_{DD}}{2} \cdot \frac{C_{gg} + C_{dd}}{\frac{W}{2L}\mu C_{ox}\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2} \end{equation}

Here \(C_{gg} + C_{dd}\) is the capacitance each stage drives (the next stage’s gate plus its own drain), and the denominator is the square-law saturation current of a device with its gate at the full supply. ([2] writes the threshold in this equation as \(V_{TH}\); it is the same \(V_T\) as below.) Observe that the delay depends on exactly the same \(\mu\) and \(V_T\) as the amplifier’s \(g_m\), so it moves with PVT in the same direction.

For the inverters in the analog signal path, the gates are biased at \(V_{DD}/2\), so their transconductance is [2]

\begin{equation} \label{eq:signal-gm} g_m = \frac{W}{L}\mu C_{ox}\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{2} - V_T\right) \end{equation}

Notice that \(V_{DD}\) directly sets the analog inverter’s \(g_m\), and thus also its unity-gain frequency

\[\omega_u = \frac{g_m}{C_{gg} + C_{dd}}, \qquad f_u = \frac{\omega_u}{2\pi}\]

We now want to express the ring frequency in terms of this same \(g_m\) [2]. The derivation takes three steps.

Step 1: Invert the stage delay. Rearranging Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-delay}, the factor of \(1/2\) in \(V_{DD}/2\) cancels the factor of 2 in \(W/2L\):

\[\frac{1}{t_p} = \frac{2}{V_{DD}} \cdot \frac{\frac{W}{2L}\mu C_{ox}\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2}{C_{gg} + C_{dd}} = \frac{W}{L}\mu C_{ox} \cdot \frac{\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2}{V_{DD}\left(C_{gg} + C_{dd}\right)}\]

Substituting into Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-frequency} gives the oscillation frequency in terms of device parameters:

\[f_{osc} = \frac{1}{2N t_p} = \frac{1}{2N} \cdot \frac{W}{L}\mu C_{ox} \cdot \frac{\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2}{V_{DD}\left(C_{gg} + C_{dd}\right)}\]

Step 2: Eliminate the device constant using the amplifier’s \(g_m\). The product \((W/L)\mu C_{ox}\) is common to the ring and the amplifier, since both use the same unit inverter. Solving Eq. \eqref{eq:signal-gm} for it,

\[\frac{W}{L}\mu C_{ox} = \frac{g_m}{\frac{V_{DD}}{2} - V_T}\]

and substituting into the previous expression gives the oscillation frequency in terms of \(g_m\) [2]:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:fosc-gm} f_{osc} = \frac{1}{2N} \cdot \frac{\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2}{V_{DD}\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{2} - V_T\right)} \cdot \frac{g_m}{C_{gg} + C_{dd}} \end{equation}

Notice that the mobility, the oxide capacitance and the device aspect ratio have all disappeared. Only the supply, the threshold and the amplifier’s own \(g_m/C\) remain.

Step 3: Write it in terms of \(f_u\). Since \(g_m/(C_{gg} + C_{dd}) = \omega_u = 2\pi f_u\),

\begin{equation} \label{eq:fosc-fu} f_{osc} = \frac{1}{2N} \cdot \alpha \cdot 2\pi f_u = \frac{\pi}{N}\,\alpha f_u \end{equation}

where all the voltage dependence is collected into a single dimensionless factor:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:alpha} \alpha = \frac{\left(V_{DD} - V_T\right)^2}{V_{DD}\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{2} - V_T\right)} \end{equation}

Eq. \eqref{eq:fosc-fu} is the central result. The ring frequency is the inverter’s unity-gain frequency multiplied by a factor that depends only weakly on the operating point. In general \(\alpha\) is a function of \(V_{DD}\). However, when \(V_{DD} \gg V_T\), the threshold terms in Eq. \eqref{eq:alpha} become negligible, and

\[\alpha \;\rightarrow\; \frac{V_{DD}^2}{V_{DD} \cdot \frac{V_{DD}}{2}} = 2, \qquad f_{osc} \;\rightarrow\; \frac{2\pi}{N} f_u\]

so \(f_{osc}\) becomes directly proportional to \(f_u\). In [2], \(V_T\) is about 150 mV and the nominal \(V_{DD}\) is 700 mV. Evaluating Eq. \eqref{eq:alpha} at that point gives \(\alpha = (0.55)^2 / (0.7 \times 0.2) \approx 2.16\), already close to the limiting value. The simulated \(\alpha\) in [2] stays within ±5% over the relevant supply range.

Notice also that the stage capacitance \(C_{gg} + C_{dd}\) appears in both \(t_p\) and \(\omega_u\). The ring therefore automatically tracks \(g_m\) per unit capacitance, which is exactly what sets the amplifier’s poles.

We can therefore tune \(V_{DD}\) with the programmable LDO to set the oscillation frequency, and holding \(f_{osc}\) constant across corners stabilizes \(f_u\). This translates into a relatively fixed pole frequency in the amplifier’s transfer function across corners [2].

MPT and MNT

One key implementation detail of the RO-based sensor in Figure 1 is the pair of triode-region devices, MPT and MNT, between the ring and its two supply rails [1]. The inverter-based amplifier sees a very small swing, so its devices are biased near mid-supply and never see the full regulated voltage across any two terminals. The inverters in the RO, on the other hand, swing rail to rail. Since the regulated voltage can reach 1.25 V across corners, an unprotected RO device would see the full supply across its terminals. MPT and MNT are added to prevent this over-voltage, keeping the voltage across any two terminals of the RO devices within the rated limit [1].

Measuring the ring frequency

Take a stable reference clock, for example 100 MHz, and open a counting window lasting \(M\) reference periods. Count the number \(N\) of RO edges inside this window:

\[N = \frac{f_{RO}}{f_{REF}/M} = \frac{M f_{RO}}{f_{REF}}\]

For example, a 2 GHz ring counted over a 150 ns window (15 periods of a 100 MHz reference) gives \(N = 300\). One count is then \(1/300 \approx 0.3\%\) of frequency. The reference crystal is accurate to parts per million, so the count is an absolute measure of this die’s speed.

The calibration loop

Now compare the measured \(N\) with a target \(N^*\):

  • If \(N > N^* + \text{margin}\), the die is too fast, so \(D\) goes down by 1. We want a smaller \(f_{osc}\), or equivalently a larger \(t_p\). Reducing \(V_{DD}\) increases \(t_p\) and lowers the oscillation frequency.
  • If \(N < N^* - \text{margin}\), the die is too slow, so \(D\) goes up by 1. We want a larger \(f_{osc}\), or a smaller \(t_p\). Increasing \(V_{DD}\) reduces \(t_p\) and raises the oscillation frequency.
  • Otherwise, the loop stops. The margin is set by the tolerance (discussed below).

Note that \(t_p\) is not strictly inversely proportional to \(V_{DD}\). From Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-delay}, \(t_p \propto V_{DD}/(V_{DD} - V_T)^2\), which decreases monotonically as \(V_{DD}\) increases. Monotonicity is all the loop needs: it guarantees that every correction moves the frequency in the intended direction.

The sign of the correction is what makes this negative feedback. A higher code gives a higher \(V_{REG}\), a faster ring, and a larger count, which makes the error larger. The rule then pushes the code back down. The correction always opposes the error, so the system works much like a thermostat.

There is a practical limit, however: the loop can only move \(V_{DD}\) as far as the supply range allows. Set the nominal \(V_{REG}\) below the maximum so that slow and hot dies have room to go up.

The programmable LDO

A digital code \(D\) sets the supply in small voltage steps:

\[V_{REG} = V_{min} + D\,\Delta V\]

The Cisco design used \(\Delta V = 8\) mV steps [3]. A subtle point is that the LDO’s absolute accuracy does not matter. Even if the reference is 20 mV off, the feedback loop simply settles at a different code \(D\), because it locks to a frequency, not to a voltage. Consequently, the regulator does not need a bandgap reference; a reference clock on the board is sufficient [3].

Choosing the design numbers

Several questions remain: how many stages should the RO have, what should the target frequency be, how is the frequency comparator built, and how is its output turned into an LDO code? The following numbers must be chosen.

Number of ring stages

As discussed above, RO power is nearly independent of the number of stages, while random variation in the oscillation frequency averages out over more stages [2]. A longer ring is therefore preferable for mismatch. It also lowers the oscillation frequency for a given stage delay (Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-frequency}), which brings the count into a convenient range. For reference, the 740 MHz nominal frequency and 5 ps stage delay quoted in [2] imply, through Eq. \eqref{eq:ro-frequency}, a ring of roughly 135 stages.

The target count \(N^*\)

There are two sensible choices:

  1. The nominal corner. Measure \(N\) at TT, 27 °C and the nominal supply, and use that as the target. This is the corner where the design has already been verified and works optimally, so the loop reproduces the verified design on every die.
  2. A performance target. Choose the ring frequency that gives the desired amplifier bandwidth. Zheng et al. set their frequency target externally for the best CTLE bandwidth, power and performance [2], and the target in the Cisco design is programmable [1], [3].

The first choice is the natural starting point; the second is a refinement once the relationship between ring frequency and amplifier bandwidth has been characterized.

Step size and tolerance

One code changes the count by

\[G = N^* \cdot S \cdot \Delta V, \qquad S = \frac{\partial \ln f}{\partial V}\]

Here \(S\) is the fractional change of ring frequency per volt, so \(S\,\Delta V\) is the fractional frequency change per code, and multiplying by \(N^*\) converts it to counts. With \(S \approx 1.7\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta V = 10\) mV, a single code changes the count by about 5.

The tolerance window around the target contains \(2\,\text{tol} + 1\) integer counts. The important point is that this window must be wider than one step:

\[2\,\text{tol} + 1 > G\]

To see why, suppose the window were narrower than one step. Then the count would jump over the window on every update. One code lands just above the window, so the loop steps down. The next code lands just below it, so the loop steps up. The loop then toggles between those two codes forever, which is a limit cycle. With the window wider than one step, at least one code always lands inside it, and the loop stops there.

Timing

During each iteration, the loop must:

  1. wait for the LDO to settle (at least \(5\tau\));
  2. count ring edges for \(M\) reference periods;
  3. compare \(N\) with \(N^*\);
  4. update \(D\).

For simulation, a counting window of a few hundred nanoseconds keeps the runtime short.

Code range

The code range must cover the slowest and hottest corners without exceeding the device voltage rating.

Biasing anything outside the regulated domain

Anything biased from outside the regulated domain must follow \(V_{REG}/2\). Either AC-couple the amplifier input, or derive its DC level from \(V_{REG}\).

The reason follows from Eq. \eqref{eq:inverter-gm}. The inverter’s trip point sits at about \(V_{REG}/2\), and the loop deliberately moves \(V_{REG}\) from corner to corner. A source with a fixed DC level is no longer at the trip point once \(V_{REG}\) moves. The high-gain inverter amplifies that DC offset, and the output saturates at some corners. AC coupling, or a DC level derived from \(V_{REG}\), keeps the input centred on the trip point wherever the loop settles. The same applies to any following stage that assumes a fixed common-mode level.

Foreground or background calibration

Decide between running the loop once at start-up (foreground) and re-checking periodically (background). In background mode, add hysteresis so that small drifts do not make the supply dither. In practice, this means a wider error threshold for restarting a correction than for stopping one.

Is the Zheng–Murmann FSM implementation required?

In the implementation of Zheng et al. [2], the ring oscillator’s output itself clocks a finite state machine (FSM). The FSM controls the LDO, which in that design regulates the ground of the core and reference circuits rather than the supply. The FSM uses an available 100 MHz reference to tune the LDO until the ring reaches a programmable frequency target (nominally 740 MHz, corresponding to a 5 ps inverter delay), with hysteresis. The target is set externally for the best CTLE bandwidth, power and performance, and the whole replica-bias block (reference diode, ring oscillator, LDO and FSM) can be shared across several transceiver channels to amortize its area and power [2].

For an ideal or behavioral feedback loop, most of these details are optional rather than necessary:

  • Clocking the FSM from the ring is a hardware convenience, not a requirement. Any controller that counts ring edges in a reference-timed window and updates the code implements the same loop. The Cisco design uses firmware instead [1].
  • Regulating ground instead of the supply is an interface choice in [2]. The Cisco design regulates the supply [1]. The sensing principle is the same either way.
  • Hysteresis is worth keeping, because it prevents dithering in background operation.
  • Sharing the bias block across channels matters only for area and power in a multi-channel chip.

What is necessary is common to both designs: a ring built from the same unit inverter on the same regulated net, a stable reference to measure its frequency against, a programmable regulator, and a controller whose correction has the right sign.

Summary

A self-biased CMOS inverter is an efficient, linear amplifier, but its \(g_m\), and with it its bandwidth, is set directly by \(V_{DD} - 2V_T\) and the device mobility, which makes it highly sensitive to PVT. A ring oscillator built from the same unit inverter oscillates at a frequency proportional to the inverter’s unity-gain frequency, \(f_{osc} = (\pi/N)\,\alpha f_u\), with \(\alpha \approx 2\). Counting the ring’s edges against a stable reference clock gives an absolute measure of the die’s speed. A programmable LDO, driven by a simple negative-feedback controller, then adjusts the supply until the count matches a target. The result is a nearly constant \(f_u\) across corners, without a bandgap and with only dynamic power spent in the sensor. Its limits are the available supply range and how closely the rail-to-rail ring tracks the amplifier biased at mid-supply.

Behavioral modeling of the DVS feedback loop in Cadence will be explored in a future post.

References

[1] K. R. Lakshmikumar, A. Kurylak, M. Nagaraju, R. Booth, R. K. Nandwana, J. Pampanin, and V. Boccuzzi, “A Process and Temperature Insensitive CMOS Linear TIA for 100 Gb/s/λ PAM-4 Optical Links,” IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 54, no. 11, pp. 3180–3190, Nov. 2019. doi:10.1109/JSSC.2019.2939652

[2] K. Zheng, Y. Frans, K. Chang, and B. Murmann, “A 56 Gb/s 6 mW 300 µm² inverter-based CTLE for short-reach PAM2 applications in 16 nm CMOS,” in Proc. IEEE Custom Integrated Circuits Conference (CICC), 2018. doi:10.1109/CICC.2018.8357076

[3] K. Lakshmikumar, A. C. Kurylak, M. Nagaraju, and R. V. H. Booth, “Process and temperature insensitive linear circuit,” U.S. Patent 10,505,509 B2, Dec. 10, 2019. Google Patents

[4] B. Razavi, RF Microelectronics, 2nd ed. Upper Saddle River, NJ, USA: Prentice Hall, 2012.

entry.title: Analog Design Using The CMOS Inverter – Part 1

link.title: Analog Design Using The CMOS Inverter – Part 1

entry.content:
Technology scaling has been extraordinarily effective for digital circuits. Smaller devices and lower supply voltages have enabled higher density and switching speed, while process development has continued to improve the trade-off between on-state current and leakage. Analog design has benefited from the same technology, but not always in the same way.

A conventional analog amplifier often relies on a large transistor output resistance to obtain voltage gain. To first order, the intrinsic gain of a MOS transistor is

\[A_{v,\mathrm{int}} = g_m r_o = \frac{g_m}{g_{ds}},\]

where $g_m$ is the transconductance and $r_o=1/g_{ds}$ is the small-signal output resistance. Short-channel effects, including channel-length modulation and drain-induced barrier lowering (discussed in my previous article), make it harder to preserve a large $r_o$ as channel lengths shrink. At the same time, the supply voltage has generally scaled faster than the threshold voltage. The available voltage headroom for stacking devices has therefore become more restrictive.

This is one reason that familiar gain-enhancement techniques, especially cascoding, have become difficult to use in low-voltage processes. A cascode can raise output resistance, but it also consumes voltage headroom and adds internal nodes and capacitances. Those extra nodes can reduce large-signal speed, even when the small-signal output resistance looks attractive. Whether a cascode is worthwhile depends on the process, bias conditions, load, and performance target; the point is that its benefits no longer look as attractive.

A CMOS inverter offers a different starting point. It contains a PMOS and an NMOS connected in a complementary push-pull arrangement, with their gates driven by the same input and their drains joined at the output. There is no cascode stack. More importantly, when the inverter is biased in its transition region, both devices conduct and both contribute transconductance. With the output capacitance held fixed, the effective transconductance is approximately

\[g_{m,\mathrm{inv}} = g_{mn}+g_{mp}.\]

The inverter can therefore provide substantial transconductance per unit of voltage headroom. This is especially useful in circuits where bandwidth and energy per transition matter more than obtaining a very large open-loop voltage gain.

The key question is how to bias the inverter in the transition region, where its transconductance is high. As a digital gate, the inverter is normally driven between the supply rails and spends most of its time near one of the two logic states. Digital designers generally avoid the center region to reduce the risk of metastability. As an analog circuit, however, the inverter is biased near the steep portion of its voltage-transfer curve, where a small change at the input produces a much larger change at the output. The same transistor pair supports both uses; the operating point determines which behavior we exploit.

A simple resistor connected from the output back to the input can establish this operating point without a separate precision bias circuit. That idea leads to several useful circuits, including inverter amplifiers, transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs), clock and data buffers, and source-series-terminated output drivers. The following sections build these applications from the inverter’s DC behavior and small-signal model.

Section I: Voltage-transfer characteristics (VTC)

What changes when the input is between the rails?

A CMOS inverter is usually introduced as a logic element: a low input produces a high output, and a high input produces a low output. The more interesting question for analog design is what happens while the input moves continuously between those two extremes.

Let the supply be $V_{DD}$, the NMOS threshold be $V_{TN}>0$, and the magnitude of the PMOS threshold be $\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$. We will initially use the long-channel square-law model. This is useful for understanding the operating regions and deriving a first estimate of the switching point, although it is not a precise device model for a modern nanoscale process.

The NMOS overdrive is

\[V_{OV,n}=V_{in}-V_{TN},\]

and the PMOS overdrive, using the magnitude convention for its threshold, is

\[V_{OV,p}=V_{DD}-V_{in}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert.\]

The NMOS begins to conduct strongly when $V_{in}$ exceeds $V_{TN}$. The PMOS remains on while $V_{in}<V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$. Between these limits, both transistors can conduct at the same time. That overlap is the operating region of interest for analog amplification.

Five regions of the inverter

Region A: NMOS nominally off, PMOS in triode. When $V_{in}<V_{TN}$, the NMOS is off in the ideal cutoff model. The PMOS is on because its gate is low, and its drain-to-source voltage is small when $V_{out}$ is close to $V_{DD}$. It therefore operates in triode and pulls the output toward the supply. In an actual transistor, subthreshold current does not abruptly become zero below threshold, so the output can begin to move slightly before the ideal threshold is reached. The amount of movement depends on leakage, loading, temperature, and the rest of the circuit.

Region B: NMOS in saturation, PMOS in triode. As $V_{in}$ rises above $V_{TN}$, the NMOS begins to pull current from the output toward ground. While the output remains high, the NMOS drain-source voltage is large relative to its overdrive, so it is in saturation. The PMOS still has a small source-drain voltage and remains in triode. Increasing the input strengthens the NMOS and reduces the PMOS overdrive, so the output starts to fall more rapidly.

Region C: both transistors in saturation. As the output falls, the PMOS source-drain voltage grows. Once it is large enough, the PMOS also enters saturation. There is then a range in which both devices conduct in saturation. This region nominally contains the steepest part of the voltage-transfer curve. A rise in $V_{in}$ increases the NMOS pull-down current and decreases the PMOS pull-up current. Both effects move the output downward. In the small-signal model, their transconductances add, which is why this region is advantageous for voltage gain and bandwidth.

Region D: NMOS in triode, PMOS in saturation. As the output falls further, the NMOS drain-source voltage eventually becomes smaller than its overdrive. The NMOS enters triode, while the PMOS can remain in saturation. The output is now close to ground, and further increases in input mainly strengthen the pull-down path.

Region E: PMOS nominally off, NMOS in triode. When $V_{in}\geq V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$, the PMOS is off in the ideal cutoff model. The NMOS pulls the output toward ground. As in Region A, practical leakage and short-channel effects soften the ideal transition.

Deriving the input trip-point

A useful first estimate of the inverter switching point, often denoted $V_M$, is the point on the VTC where the input and output are equal:

\[V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M.\]

At this point, the output voltage is not being forced high or low. The NMOS pull-down current and PMOS pull-up current have equal magnitudes. Under the square-law saturation model,

\[I_{D,n}=\frac{1}{2}\beta_n(V_M-V_{TN})^2,\] \[\lvert I_{D,p}\rvert=\frac{1}{2}\beta_p(V_{DD}-V_M-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert)^2,\]

where

\[\beta_n=\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n, \qquad \beta_p=\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_p.\]

The parameters $\mu_n$ and $\mu_p$ are the carrier mobilities in the NMOS and PMOS, $C_{ox}$ is the oxide capacitance per unit area, and $W/L$ is the device aspect ratio. Current balance requires:

\[\frac{1}{2}\beta_n(V_M-V_{TN})^2 = \frac{1}{2}\beta_p(V_{DD}-V_M-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert)^2.\]

Cancel the $1/2$ factor and take the square root, and we get:

\[\sqrt{\beta_n}(V_M-V_{TN}) = \sqrt{\beta_p}(V_{DD}-V_M-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert).\]

Expanding the right-hand side and collecting the $V_M$ terms gives:

\[V_M(\sqrt{\beta_n}+\sqrt{\beta_p}) = \sqrt{\beta_n}V_{TN} +\sqrt{\beta_p}(V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert).\]

Therefore, the square-law estimate of the switching voltage is

\[{ V_M= \frac{\sqrt{\beta_n}V_{TN}+\sqrt{\beta_p}(V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert)} {\sqrt{\beta_n}+\sqrt{\beta_p}} }\]

This expression is a weighted average of the NMOS turn-on voltage, $V_{TN}$, and the PMOS turn-off voltage, $V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$. The weights are the square roots of the transistor strength parameters. A stronger NMOS pulls the switching point downward; a stronger PMOS pulls it upward.

It is worth being careful with the overdrive notation here. The NMOS and PMOS do not generally have the same overdrive. Equating $\tfrac{1}{2}\mu C_{ox}V_{OV}^2$ for both devices without distinguishing their overdrives would omit both device sizing and the different distances from the input voltage to each threshold. The current-balance derivation above retains those differences.

The limiting cases are intuitive:

  • If $\beta_n\gg\beta_p$, the NMOS is much stronger, and $V_M\rightarrow V_{TN}$.

  • If $\beta_n\ll\beta_p$, the PMOS is much stronger, and $V_M\rightarrow V_{DD}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$.

  • If the effective strengths are comparable, the switching point lies between these limits. It is exactly at $V_{DD}/2$ only when the device strengths and threshold magnitudes satisfy the required symmetry.

Since $\beta$ includes mobility as well as geometry, equal $W/L$ does not automatically mean equal drive strength. The analog sizing optimum can also differ from the digital sizing optimum: in digital use, designers often size the PMOS wider to balance rise and fall delays; in an inverter biased for analog operation, the relevant target may instead be transconductance per input capacitance, noise, linearity, or output swing. There is no universal PMOS-to-NMOS width ratio. The mobility ratio, device architecture, layout parasitics, and PVT corners all matter.

For short-channel devices, the square-law expression should be read as intuition rather than sign-off mathematics. Velocity saturation, mobility degradation, DIBL, body effect, and non-ideal output conductance change the current equations. In practice, the DC bias point and maximum gain should be extracted from the PDK model and verified across corners and mismatch.

An important trade-off is that there is a balance between the transconductance of the inverter—or how steep the VTC is—and how much input swing it can tolerate while operating linearly. However, in most receiver applications, like the TIA in an optical link, the input swing is low enough and higher gain is prioritized over linearity.

Boundaries of the saturated region (Region C)

The labels $V_{TOP}$ and $V_{BOT}$ are useful when describing the output-voltage interval over which both transistors remain saturated for a given input bias $V_G$.

For the NMOS, saturation requires

\[V_{DS,n}\geq V_{GS,n}-V_{TN}.\]

Using $V_{DS,n}=V_{out}$ and $V_{GS,n}=V_G$ gives

\[V_{out}\geq V_G-V_{TN}.\]

At equality, the NMOS is just at the boundary between saturation and triode. Define this lower boundary as

\[{V_{BOT}=V_G-V_{TN}.}\]

For the PMOS, saturation requires

\[V_{SD,p}\geq V_{SG,p}-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert.\]

Since $V_{SD,p}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$ and $V_{SG,p}=V_{DD}-V_G$, this becomes

\[V_{DD}-V_{out}\geq V_{DD}-V_G-\lvert V_{TP}\rvert,\]

or

\[V_{out}\leq V_G+\lvert V_{TP}\rvert.\]

At equality, the PMOS is just at the saturation-to-triode boundary. Define the upper boundary as

\[{V_{TOP}=V_G+\lvert V_{TP}\rvert.}\]

Thus, at a fixed input bias $V_G$, the output lies in the both-saturated interval when

\[{V_G-V_{TN}\leq V_{out}\leq V_G+\lvert V_{TP}\rvert.}\]

These are output-voltage boundaries evaluated for a fixed input bias. They should not be mistaken for universal input-voltage breakpoints on the entire VTC, because each region boundary depends on both $V_{in}$ and $V_{out}$. The width of this idealized output interval is $V_{TN}+\lvert V_{TP}\rvert$, provided the chosen bias actually turns both devices on and the supply permits such an interval.

Transfer function in Region C

Around a DC operating point, a small input perturbation can be represented by $v_{in}$ and the corresponding output perturbation by $v_{out}$. The small-signal drain currents caused by the changing gate voltage are approximately $g_{mn}v_{in}$ for the NMOS and $g_{mp}v_{in}$ for the PMOS. Although the devices have complementary polarities, both incremental effects pull the output in the same direction when the input rises: the NMOS draws more current from the output, while the PMOS supplies less current to it.

Consequently, the inverter’s effective transconductance is

\[g_{m,\mathrm{inv}}=g_{mn}+g_{mp}.\]

If the output resistance of the two devices is $r_{on}$ and $r_{op}$, the unloaded small-signal output resistance is approximately

\[r_{out}=r_{on}\parallel r_{op}.\]

Ignoring additional loads for the moment, its low-frequency voltage gain is

\[{A_v=-(g_{mn}+g_{mp})(r_{on}\parallel r_{op}).}\]

The minus sign reflects the inverter’s inverting behavior. With a load conductance $G_L$ and a load capacitance $C_L$, the one-pole approximation is

\[A_v(s)=- \frac{g_{mn}+g_{mp}} {g_{ds,n}+g_{ds,p}+G_L+sC_L}.\]

This expression shows the central advantage and the central limitation at once. Adding the PMOS transconductance can raise the numerator, but the attainable gain is still limited by the output conductance and the loading. The same input also drives both transistor gates, so the input capacitance includes contributions from both devices and their gate-drain parasitics.

The inverter is not automatically the best amplifier for every application. Its gain is sensitive to the operating point, its transfer curve is nonlinear, and both devices conduct DC current while it is biased in the transition region. Its appeal is strongest when low-voltage operation, high transconductance, compactness, and speed outweigh the need for high open-loop gain or very low static power.

Noise deserves a careful treatment. For a simple MOS channel thermal-noise model, each device contributes a drain-current noise density proportional to $4kT\gamma g_m$. If the two uncorrelated channel-noise currents are referred to the input through the combined transconductance, the simplified input-referred voltage-noise density scales approximately as

\[S_{v,in}= \frac{4kT(\gamma_n g_{mn}+\gamma_p g_{mp})} {(g_{mn}+g_{mp})^2}.\]

Under the assumptions of this model, increasing combined transconductance can reduce input-referred thermal voltage noise. However, one must confirm this with simulations, as the ideal model does not include bias current, flicker noise, source impedance, load, device sizing, noise transfer from internal nodes, and the actual topology.

Section II: Self-biasing with resistive feedback

Why a bias circuit is needed

As discussed in the preceding sections, the inverter has its greatest small-signal gain near its switching point, but a bare inverter does not provide a convenient independent DC bias input. If we simply apply a DC input voltage, small changes in device threshold, mobility, or supply can shift the operating point. A precision external reference and bias network could be added, but that consumes area, power, and voltage headroom and can complicate a high-speed signal path. Adding a complicated precision bias circuit would reintroduce many of the problems that the inverter approach is intended to avoid.

A resistor $R_F$ from output to input offers a compact alternative. At DC, a MOS gate draws negligible current in the ideal model. If the input is otherwise not connected to a DC source, essentially no DC current flows through $R_F$, and therefore the voltage drop across it is zero:

\[I_{R_F,DC}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_{in,DC}= V_{out,DC}.\]

The DC operating point must therefore lie near the intersection of the inverter VTC and the line $V_{out}=V_{in}$. That is the switching point $V_M$, where both devices conduct and the magnitude of the local slope is usually high.

The feedback action is intuitive. Suppose the input node is perturbed upward. The inverter output moves downward. Through $R_F$, that lower output pulls the input node back down. The feedback opposes the original perturbation and stabilizes the DC operating point. In other words, the resistor turns the inverter’s own transfer curve into its bias mechanism.

The precise bias is not guaranteed to equal the square-law $V_M$ derived earlier. Finite DC input currents, leakage, other resistors, an attached source, asymmetry, and non-ideal device models can shift it. The practical design target is a stable point near the high-gain portion of the measured or simulated VTC.

Small-signal behavior with feedback

The feedback resistor also changes the AC behavior. Use the inverter small-signal model with combined transconductance $g_m=g_{mn}+g_{mp}$, output resistance $r_o$, and total output capacitance $C_L$. Let the input-node small-signal voltage be $v_x$ and the output voltage be $v_o$. Applying KCL at the output node gives

\[g_m v_x+\frac{v_o}{r_o}+sC_Lv_o =\frac{v_x-v_o}{R_F}.\]

Rearrange to collect the output terms:

\[v_o\left(\frac{1}{r_o}+sC_L+\frac{1}{R_F}\right) =v_x\left(\frac{1}{R_F}-g_m\right).\]

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $R_F$ yields

\[{ \frac{v_o}{v_x} =\frac{1-g_mR_F} {1+R_F/r_o+sR_FC_L} }.\]

This model assumes the input node is driven by a sufficiently low-impedance small-signal source, so $v_x$ can be treated as the input variable. The expression contains one dominant output pole, set by the parallel combination $R_F \parallel r_o$ driving the load capacitance $C_L$. Its 3-dB bandwidth is

\[\omega_{3\mathrm{dB}} =\frac{1+R_F/r_o}{R_FC_L} =\frac{1}{r_oC_L}+\frac{1}{R_FC_L}.\]

Without feedback, the corresponding one-pole approximation is

\[\omega_{3\mathrm{dB},0}=\frac{1}{r_oC_L}.\]

The resistor adds a conductance of $1/R_F$ at the output. In other words, the feedback resistor is in shunt with the output impedance, so the effective output impedance driving the load capacitance is smaller, and the dominant pole moves upward! This is the small-signal explanation for how resistive feedback can extend bandwidth and can be used in high-speed designs. However, this is only an approximation, because input capacitance, finite source impedance, gate-drain capacitance, and additional internal poles must be included in the simulation for an exact value of the 3-dB bandwidth.

There is also a trade-off here. The same feedback path that reduces the effective output resistance also changes the closed-loop gain and loads the input/output nodes. A smaller $R_F$ gives stronger feedback and more bandwidth extension, but it can reduce signal gain, increase current through the feedback path, and alter linearity and output swing. A larger $R_F$ reduces AC loading but weakens the bandwidth and bias-restoration effects. The best value depends on the target gain, input/output impedances, capacitances, and data rate.

With feedback, the input resistance seen by an input current is reduced approximately by the loop gain. If $A$ is the magnitude of the inverter’s voltage gain, then a useful first-order estimate is

\[{R_{in}=\frac{R_F}{1+A}.}\]

The intuition is that feedback makes the input node move much less than it would without the amplifier. A small input voltage is needed to accommodate a given input current, so the input appears low impedance. This is especially useful in a TIA, where the photodiode capacitance would otherwise create a low-frequency input pole.

The main advantage of the feedback resistor is that it provides three useful functions in one component: it establishes the DC operating point, implements negative feedback in the signal path, and provides a design knob for bandwidth and gain. Since the inverter uses one PMOS and one NMOS rather than a multi-device stack, it also preserves voltage headroom and can exploit both transconductances.

For applications that require only AC amplification, it is common to isolate the external signal’s DC level with an input coupling capacitor. The feedback resistor then establishes the internal bias independently of the external signal common-mode voltage.

References

  1. Analog Circuits by Prof. Shanti Pavan on YouTube. Watch the video.

  2. W. Bae, “CMOS Inverter as Analog Circuit: An Overview,” Journal of Low Power Electronics and Applications, vol. 9, no. 3, article 26, 2019. https://doi.org/10.3390/jlpea9030026

  3. B. Razavi, “Fifty Applications of the CMOS Inverter—Parts 1–5 [The Analog Mind],” IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine.

link.title: MOSFET Device Behavior for Circuit Designers

entry.content:
Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors, or MOSFETs, are used extensively in modern chip designs, because they allow high device density and low power dissipation. As this technology lends itself to digital integrated circuits well, it has become a necessity for analog designers to design high-precision, low-noise, and wideband circuits with MOSFETs rather than bipolar transistors (such as BJTs) and other technologies which have better performance characteristics for analog circuits than MOSFETs — such as higher transconductance for the same bias current, lower noise, etc. Therefore, it is necessary to study the fundamental behavior of MOSFET devices to gain the intuition for using them appropriately in larger circuits.

MOSFET Channel Formation

The cross section of a typical NMOS device is shown above. Two heavily n-doped regions, called the Source (S) and the Drain (D), sit within a p-type substrate which is also called the Body (B). Between the source and the drain is the region which has the potential to form a channel. The Gate (G) is a conductor that sits above the channel region, and the gate-source voltage can be used to control the conductance of the channel underneath.

Now suppose you connect the source terminal to GND, and the gate is connected to a source \(V_G\). As long as \(V_{GS}=V_{G}-V_{S}=0\), there is no channel formation under the gate, since there are no mobile charges that can move from the source to the drain.

Notice that the source and drain both contain p-n junctions, with the substrate being the p-type and the n-wells being the n-type. Recall that:

  • the p-type bulk has holes as majority mobile carriers, plus fixed −ve ionized acceptors.
  • the n-wells have electrons as majority mobile carriers, plus fixed +ve ionized donors.

When a small positive voltage \(V_{GS}\) is applied, the positive charge on the gate pushes holes away from the channel, leaving behind a region of negatively charged ionized acceptors — the technical term for this is the depletion region. This depletion region has fewer mobile holes than before.

As we continue to increase the gate voltage \(V_{GS}\) further, something more interesting happens. The electric field from the gate becomes strong enough to attract the minority electrons in the substrate towards the surface beneath the gate. Eventually a point is reached where the electron concentration is larger than the hole concentration at the surface, and the depletion region completely “inverts” and becomes n-type — creatively, this is called inversion.

Thus, when the surface electron concentration becomes comparable to or greater than the hole concentration, we have an inversion region. With sufficiently large \(V_{GS}\), a continuous sheet of electrons forms between the source and the drain. This is the MOSFET channel.

Notice that the gate voltage can be used as a knob to directly control or tune the electron concentration in the channel. The electrons in the channel come primarily from the heavily doped n-type source/drain regions. The role of the gate is simply to establish an electric field at the surface underneath that makes an electron-rich channel energetically favorable.

Thus the MOSFET goes from OFF → depletion → inversion with increasing \(V_{GS}\).

The Threshold Voltage

The gate-source voltage \(V_{GS}\) required to produce an inversion region is called the threshold voltage, \(V_{th}\). The exact value of this can be calculated by solving for the work functions of the materials involved, but for all practical purposes, it is a circuit-level marker for the onset of strong inversion and is usually provided by the foundry and found through simulation.

Once \(V_{GS}>V_{th}\), there is a substantial amount of electrons available at the surface, and the amount of inversion charge can be approximated (using \(Q=CV\)) as:

\[Q_{inv}=-C_{ox}(V_{GS}-V_{th})\]

It is worth pointing out here that this equation suggests the fundamental operating principle of MOSFETs: the amount of charge (and therefore current) sitting in the channel is directly controlled by the gate voltage. The MOSFET acts like a voltage-controlled current source.

Now connect the drain D to a positive voltage and keep the source S at ground. The channel electrons experience a lateral electric field and drift toward the drain. Thus the current (conventional) flows from drain to source.

Deriving the Current Equation

To derive the actual channel current equation, we start from the inversion charge after \(V_{DS}\) has been applied, and remind ourselves that the channel voltage isn’t exactly zero everywhere. The channel voltage, \(V(x)\), starts at approximately 0 at the source and reaches \(V_{DS}\) at the drain. Therefore, the effective local inversion charge becomes:

\[Q_{inv}(x)=-C_{ox}(V_{GS}-V_{th}-V(x))\]

Before we proceed, it is useful to define the overdrive voltage (\(V_{OV}\)) as

\[V_{OV} = V_{GS}-V_{th}\]

The drain current is equal to the inversion charge times the carrier velocity in the n-channel, times the width, since everything is expressed as line densities. We know from electromagnetics that

\[v_n=\mu_n E_x\]

and

\[E_x=-\frac{dV}{dx}\]

Thus we can combine the two equations to find:

\[I_{DS}=W\, Q_{inv}\, v_n=W\left(-C_{ox}(V_{GS}-V_{th}-V(x))\right)\frac{dV}{dx}\]

Rearranging this gives:

\[I_{DS}\,dx=-\mu_{n}C_{ox} W (V_{OV} - V(x))\,dV\]

We do this integral across the channel, so \(x\) traverses from 0 to \(L\) (channel length) and therefore \(V\) changes from 0 to \(V_{DS}\). Therefore:

\[I_{DS}=-\mu_{n}C_{ox} \frac{W}{L}\left(V_{OV} V_{DS} - \dfrac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)\]

And that is the fundamental MOSFET drain current equation.

Triode/Linear Region

When \(V_{DS}\) is much smaller than \(V_{OV}\), the square term in the equation becomes irrelevant:

\[I_{DS}=-\mu_{n}C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} V_{OV} V_{DS} = R_{DS}\,V_{DS}\]

Thus the MOSFET looks like a resistor whose resistance is controlled by \(V_{OV}\). Increasing \(V_{GS}\) puts more electrons in the channel, thereby reducing the resistance.

Saturation Region

Now, what happens if we continue increasing \(V_{DS}\)? The quadratic term can no longer be ignored, obviously, but more importantly, notice that the inversion charge at the drain keeps decreasing:

\[Q_{inv}(x=L)=-C_{ox}(V_{GS}-V_{th}-V_{DS})\]

Eventually, when the drain-source voltage becomes equal to the overdrive voltage, the local charge at the drain end becomes completely zero. That is, when \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\):

\[Q_{inv}(x=L)=-C_{ox}(V_{GS}-V_{th}-V_{DS})=0\]

This is the physical origin of pinch-off, or the saturation condition. The word “saturation” can be slightly misleading if you don’t think about it physically. Pinch-off does not mean that the drain current becomes zero at the drain end, but that the inversion region reverts to being a depletion region. The electrons traveling through the channel reach this depleted region and are swept across it by the strong electric field into the drain.

Increasing \(V_{DS}\) further mainly extends the pinch-off region into the channel rather than substantially increasing the channel current. The channel current therefore becomes less dependent on \(V_{DS}\) and is now controlled primarily by \(V_{OV}\).

To summarize, the transistor enters saturation (SAT) when

\[V_{DS}\geq V_{OV},\]

and substituting the pinch-off condition into the current equation gives:

\[I_{DS}=-\frac{1}{2}\mu_{n}C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} V_{OV}^2\]

This is the famous saturated current equation. The drain current depends on the square of \(V_{OV}\), making it a “square-law” device. We can intuitively understand the equation above in the following way:

  • \(V_{OV}\) determines how much inversion charge you have.
  • \(\frac{W}{L}\) determines how effectively that charge can conduct between source and drain.

The parameters \(\mu_n\) and \(C_{ox}\) are set by the process and are out of the designer’s control.

In essence, the large-signal model for the MOSFET device is a voltage-controlled current source, as shown below.

Transconductance

How much drain current can a given change in \(V_{GS}\) produce? We find this by differentiating with respect to \(V_{GS}\) to find the transconductance of the device:

\[g_{m}= \frac{dI_{DS}}{dV_{GS}} = \mu_{n}C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} V_{OV}.\]

This is equivalent to

\[g_{m}= \frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}}.\]

The transconductance connects device physics directly to circuit design, and is therefore one of the most useful parameters in analog design. Reducing \(V_{OV}\) gives you higher \(g_m\), but increasing \(V_{OV}\) gives you more voltage headroom and a larger signal range/swing. Since \(V_{OV}\) itself is a difficult parameter to control in real designs (the threshold voltage is not really well-defined), we design our circuits based on the parameter \(\frac{g_m}{I_D}\), which is more controllable in simulation. Future posts will explore the practical procedure for the \(\frac{g_m}{I_D}\) design methodology.

It is good to memorize the entire operational flow as below:

  1. Gate electric field pushes holes away.
  2. Depletion region forms at the surface.
  3. Inversion occurs when \(V_{GS}>V_{th}\).
  4. Channel is formed.
  5. \(V_{DS}\) causes a lateral electric field.
  6. Channel electrons drift from source to drain.
  7. Channel pinches off when \(V_{DS} > V_{OV}\).
  8. Saturation.

Now, based on the two equations above, we can try to plot the I-V curves for the MOSFET model.

For small \(V_{DS}\) the MOSFET begins to act linearly, and eventually flattens out once \(V_{DS}\geq V_{OV}\). Notice that while the ideal plots show the current saturating completely after \(V_{DS}\geq V_{OV}\), the actual observed plot does not flatten out completely. This is primarily because of channel length modulation, which we study next.

Channel Length Modulation

Earlier, in the ideal long-channel model, once the drain end pinches off, we pretended that \(V_{DS}\) no longer plays a role in affecting the current.

Realistically, increasing \(V_{DS}\) makes the depletion region around the drain extend farther toward the source (because the pinch-off condition is met before \(x=L\)). The junction becomes more reverse-biased, and the depletion region widens. This depletion region eats into the channel from the drain side, so the effective channel becomes shorter, and a shorter channel produces more current and is less resistive.

The effective length can be defined as

\[L_{eff}= L - \delta L.\]

Therefore,

\[I_{DS}=-\frac{1}{2}\mu_{n}C_{ox} \frac{W}{L- \delta L} V_{OV}^2\]

Thus, as \(\delta L\) increases, the effective length decreases and \(I_D\) increases. For small \(\frac{\delta L}{L}\):

\[\frac{1}{L- \delta L}=\frac{1}{L}\left( \frac{1}{1-\frac{\delta L}{L}} \right) \approx\frac{1}{L}\left(1+\frac{\delta L}{L}\right)\]

The change in channel length \(\delta L\) is approximately proportional to the additional drain voltage (once linearized), so we can write:

\[I_D=I_{D,sat}(1+\lambda V_{DS})\]

where \(\lambda\) is the channel length modulation factor.

This means the transistor is still in saturation, but \(I_D\) now has a finite dependence on \(V_{DS}\), making the output characteristic no longer completely flat, as shown in the I-V curve earlier.

We can find this slope by computing:

\[g_{ds}= \frac{\delta I_D}{\delta V_{DS}}= \lambda I_{D,sat} \implies r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_D}\]

In short-channel devices (nanometer nodes), the fraction \(\frac{\delta L}{L}\) becomes larger for the same \(\delta L\), since \(L\) is smaller — this means CLM needs to be carefully considered when designing circuits. For instance, the equation above shows us that \(r_o\) of the device will no longer be infinite (the ideal case), but will be limited by drain current and CLM.

In practice, whenever you care about voltage gain, current source accuracy, current mirrors, or output impedance, \(r_o\) matters. Channel length modulation directly limits the intrinsic gain of your MOSFET device, and this is more pronounced in modern processes where the channel length is under 100 nm.

Channel length modulation is only the beginning of short-channel effects. The fundamental assumption of the long-channel MOSFET was that the gate alone controls the channel current and electric field. This breaks down when \(L\) shrinks, because the depletion regions of the reverse-biased p-n junctions at the source and drain now occupy a larger portion of the channel length itself, meaning the electric fields from the drain and source also influence the channel’s charge movement.

Short-Channel Effects: Drain-Induced Barrier Lowering (DIBL)

Drain-Induced Barrier Lowering (DIBL) is, at its core, a loss of gate control in a short-channel MOSFET.

Start from a long-channel NMOS. With \(V_{GS}<V_{th}\), the gate creates a potential barrier near the source that prevents electrons in the source from entering the channel. The gate essentially controls this barrier.

As \(L\) becomes small, the drain gets physically close to the source, so when \(V_{DS}\) increases, the drain’s electric field and depletion region extend farther into the channel than they used to. Some of the drain’s electrostatic influence therefore reaches the source-side barrier.

So, for the same \(V_{GS}\), more mobile carriers are able to pass through the barrier and flow into the channel, effectively reducing the threshold voltage. The drain voltage basically helps turn the transistor ON, and electrons can be injected from the source at a lower \(V_{GS}\). Thus, \(V_{th}\) decreases as \(V_{DS}\) increases.

Recall that in subthreshold, current increases exponentially with \(V_{OV}\). This is why DIBL is a challenge for low-power designs, because even when the transistor is OFF, a high drain voltage can substantially increase leakage current.

Short-Channel Effects: Velocity Saturation

Our original derivation of the current equation assumed \(v_n=\mu_{n}E\), which is approximately true when the field is small. At high electric fields, however, electrons scatter more strongly with the lattice in the substrate, and their velocity begins to saturate instead of continuing to increase linearly with \(E\).

Thus we can rederive the current equation with:

\[I_{D} = W \cdot Q_{inv}\cdot v_{sat} =W \cdot C_{ox} \cdot v_{sat} \cdot V_{OV}\]

The current no longer follows a square law with \(V_{OV}\), and looks more linear in overdrive. At sufficiently short channel lengths, carrier velocity saturation makes the \(I_D\)–\(V_{GS}\) relationship linear instead of quadratic.

The transconductance also saturates:

\[g_{m}= \frac{dI_{DS}}{dV_{GS}}=W\,C_{ox}\, v_{sat}\]

A typical transfer characteristic shows three regions:

  • OFF: no current.
  • Subthreshold: current is dominated by diffusion leakage and increases exponentially with \(V_{OV}\).
  • Moderate inversion: the device obeys the square law approximately.
  • Strong inversion: \(I_D\) starts to increase more linearly with \(V_{OV}\) due to velocity saturation.

Summary of Operating Regions

It is useful to think of the MOSFET both from the perspective of I-V transitions (OFF/linear/saturation) and from the standpoint of device physics (strong/weak inversion, etc.). The following table (copy-pasted from ChatGPT) summarizes the previous discussion quite well.

Operating region Definition / condition Current / operation characteristic Pros Cons Typical applications / avoid
Deep subthreshold VGS well below VTH; inversion charge is extremely small Diffusion-dominated; ID changes exponentially with VOV; very small current Extremely high gm/ID; very low static power Very low speed; leakage/variation become important; poor drive capability Use: ultra-low-power sensors, always-on circuits, biomedical, energy harvesting. Avoid: high-speed signal paths
Weak inversion VGS≲VTH; weak inversion layer exists Mainly diffusion; ID remains approximately exponential in VGS; gm/ID≈1/(nUT) Excellent current efficiency; useful gm at very low current Limited bandwidth/current drive; sensitive to VTH, temperature, mismatch Use: low-power analog, sensor interfaces, bias circuits. Avoid: demanding high-speed/RF circuits
Moderate inversion Transition between weak and strong inversion Drift and diffusion both contribute; square-law and pure exponential models are both inaccurate Good compromise between gm/ID, speed, power, noise, and linearity Requires more accurate models; operating point can be less intuitive Use: low-power OTAs, amplifiers, ADCs, precision analog. Often a useful design region
Strong inversion VGS>VTH with substantial inversion charge Drift-dominated; high channel charge and current capability High gm, high current drive, better speed; familiar circuit behavior Lower gm/ID; higher power; short-channel effects become important Use: high-speed analog, RF, ADC front ends, digital logic. Avoid: when extreme energy efficiency is the primary constraint
OFF / cutoff Ideally VGS<VTH, with negligible ID In practice, subthreshold and other leakage currents remain Very low static current; useful for switching Leakage increases in nanometer CMOS; DIBL can worsen OFF current Use: digital logic and power gating. Important: “OFF” does not mean ID=0
Triode / linear Strong inversion with approximately VDS<VGS−VTH Continuous channel from source to drain; approximately voltage-controlled resistor: Ron≈1/[μCox(W/L)VOV] Useful switching behavior; low Ron; can implement variable resistance Ron depends on signal and VTH, causing distortion Use: transmission gates, analog switches, sample-and-hold, switched-capacitor circuits. Avoid: precision current-source operation
Saturation Classical condition VDS≥VGS−VTH in strong inversion Drain-end channel charge approaches zero; current becomes primarily controlled by VGS Enables voltage-to-current conversion; useful for gain and current sources ro is finite; in nanoscale CMOS, velocity saturation, CLM, DIBL and mobility degradation strongly modify behavior Use: amplifiers, current sources, differential pairs, active loads. Important: nanometer “saturation” is not the ideal textbook saturation

References

Notes from ECE 483 Analog IC Design (Prof. Pavan Kumar Hanumolu) @ UIUC.

Gray, P. R., Hurst, P. J., Lewis, S. H., & Meyer, R. G. (2009). Analysis and Design of Analog Integrated Circuits (5th ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
